title: Introduction to TypeScript
subtitle: Typed JavaScript — catch errors before they reach runtime
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: JavaScript is dynamically typed — you can pass a string where a number was expected, and the bug only surfaces at runtime (or in a user's browser). Large codebases become hard to maintain when you can't tell what type a function expects.
whyItExists.solution: TypeScript adds optional static types. You annotate variables and function parameters with types. The TypeScript compiler (tsc) checks your code before it runs and catches type mismatches at compile time — before any user sees them.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any project with more than one developer, any codebase that will be maintained for more than a few months, any library or SDK being published for others to use.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Quick one-off scripts, small personal projects, or when you're prototyping and want maximum speed — plain JS is fine. TypeScript adds a compilation step.

explainModes.beginner: TypeScript is JavaScript with labels. You tell the computer 'this variable holds a number' or 'this function returns a string'. Then the computer checks every place you use them — and warns you before you run the code if you make a mistake. Like spell-check for code logic.
explainModes.simple: TypeScript compiles to JavaScript (tsc file.ts → file.js). Type annotation: let age: number = 25. TypeScript infers types too: let name = 'Alice' is automatically string. Type error: let x: number = 'hello' — caught at compile time, not runtime. tsconfig.json configures the compiler. Use .ts for TypeScript files.
explainModes.standard: TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript — valid JS is valid TS. Types exist only at compile time; emitted JS has no types. Type inference: TS infers the type from the initial value, so you usually don't need to annotate obvious cases. Explicit annotation overrides inference. The any type disables type checking for a variable (escape hatch, avoid). Type widening: TypeScript infers the most general compatible type.
explainModes.technical: TypeScript compiles to ES5/ES6/ESNext (configurable in tsconfig.json target field). Declaration files (.d.ts) describe types for JS libraries. Definitely Typed (@types/lodash etc.) provides community-maintained declarations. tsc --strict enables all strict checks. structuralTyping: TypeScript uses structural (duck) typing, not nominal typing — if object A has all the properties type T requires, A is compatible with T, even if A wasn't explicitly declared as T.
explainModes.deepDive: TypeScript's type system is Turing-complete — you can compute types from types using conditional types, mapped types, and template literal types. Type narrowing with control flow analysis: after if (typeof x === 'string'), TS knows x is string in that branch. Project references allow splitting a large codebase into independently-compiled pieces. Incremental compilation (--incremental flag) caches the compilation for fast rebuilds. Language server protocol: TypeScript's language server powers IDE features (autocomplete, go-to-definition, rename, inline type display) in VS Code and other editors.

content.text: TypeScript types are ERASED when compiled to JavaScript. They add zero runtime overhead — the output JS is exactly what your browser runs.

questions.question: When does TypeScript catch type errors?
options: At runtime, when the code runs in the browser
At compile time, before the code runs
Only in production, not in development
TypeScript doesn't catch errors, it just documents types
questions.explanation: TypeScript catches type errors at compile time — when tsc compiles your .ts file. This means you (or your IDE) see the error immediately when writing code, before running it. The compiled JavaScript is plain JS with no type-checking at runtime.

faq.q: Do I need to annotate every variable in TypeScript?
faq.a: No! TypeScript infers types from initial values. let count = 0 is automatically typed as number. You only need annotations when inference can't determine the type (function parameters are a common case), or when you want to be explicit for documentation purposes.

tsconfig.json configures the TypeScript compiler. Key options: target (which JS version to emit: ES5, ES2020), strict (enable all strict checks — always use this), outDir (where to put compiled JS), include/exclude (which files to compile). Run tsc --init to generate a starter tsconfig.
